fixes.explanation: Verse 4 says, “…in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword.” Wormwood is a plant known for its bitter taste. The honey comes first and the bitter comes last, so the father wants his son to look at the end of the road. Verse 3 says her lips drip honey, friend, but that's only where it starts.
The father never says she is lonely. He says that in the end she is bitter as wormwood, and sharp as a double-edged sword. The text stays with bitter, so we stay with it too.

The city gate isn't where the father says her feet go. Verse 5 says, “Her feet go down to death…” Her steps lead straight to Sheol, the realm of the dead. It's a serious picture, so I'll say it plainly, friend.

Right, friend. Verse 6 says, “She does not consider the path of life; she does not know that her ways are unstable.” So she does not consider the path of life at all. The father adds that her ways are unstable, and she doesn't know it.

Yes, friend. Verse 9 warns, “…lest you concede your vigor to others, and your years to one who is cruel…” Both his vigor and his years are at stake, and the father doesn't want them handed over. That's why he says to keep far away in verse 8.

The text says the opposite. In the father's warning, the groaning son says, “I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly.” It isn't happening out of sight, friend. It's in the midst of the whole assembly.

That's right, friend. In the father's warning, the groaning son says, “I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly.” It's not hidden at all. It happens in the midst of the whole assembly, and it's a heavy line.
